content: Nusa Penida is a rugged island south-east of Bali, a 30-minute fast-boat from Sanur. Highlights: Kelingking Beach (the famous T-Rex-shaped cliff), Angel's Billabong, Broken Beach, Diamond Beach, Crystal Bay for snorkelling with manta rays. Roads are steep and narrow — hire a local driver rather than a scooter unless experienced. Day trip is possible but rushed; 2 nights is better.

Nusa Lembongan is Nusa Penida's smaller, gentler neighbour — 30 minutes from Sanur by fast-boat. Highlights: Devil's Tear (dramatic waves and blowholes), Dream Beach, mangrove tours, and the yellow suspension bridge to Nusa Ceningan. Much slower pace than Bali; good for a 2–3 night couple's / family stopover.

Tanah Lot is a Hindu temple on a small rocky islet off Bali's west coast, ~30 km from Denpasar. Access is only possible at low tide across a rock causeway — the temple itself is off-limits to non-worshippers. Sunset is the classic time to visit but it gets very crowded; arrive 90 minutes before sunset for a good photo spot. Small entry fee (~75k IDR foreigner).

Pura Luhur Uluwatu sits on a 70-metre cliff on the southern tip of Bali — one of the six major sea temples. The daily Kecak fire dance at sunset (starts around 18:00, book ahead) is a compact retelling of the Ramayana with chanting and fire. Watch out for macaque monkeys who steal sunglasses and phones — remove and pocket everything before entering.

The Sacred Monkey Forest Sanctuary in Ubud is home to ~700 long-tailed macaques living around three ancient temples in a river gorge. Entry ~80k IDR foreigner. Rules: no plastic bags, no food, no eye contact with the alpha males, no fast movements. Toddlers should be carried — the monkeys can be aggressive.

Tegalalang Rice Terraces, ~15 minutes north of Ubud, are Bali's most-photographed rice fields — cascading levels carved into a valley. Free entry to the walking path, though local farmers ask for a small 'donation' (10–20k IDR is fair). The famous Bali swings and 'love nest' installations add to the crowds. Go before 9 AM to avoid tour buses.

Lake Toba (Danau Toba) is the world's largest volcanic lake, formed by a supervolcanic eruption ~74,000 years ago. Samosir Island in the middle is the traditional home of the Batak people and the base for most travellers. Fly into Kualanamu (Medan · KNO) or Silangit (DTB · closer). Peaceful, cool, few crowds — a great non-Bali Indonesia experience.

Tana Toraja (Toraja Land) is a highland region of South Sulawesi known for its dramatic funeral rites, boat-shaped tongkonan houses, and cliff-face gravesites. Traditional funerals are open to respectful visitors — bring cigarettes/candies as gifts for the family and dress modestly. Access via Makassar (UPG) then an 8-hour drive north to Rantepao. Culturally unique — very different from Bali or Java.

Bunaken Marine Park, off Manado (MDC), is one of Indonesia's premier diving destinations. Wall dives with reef sharks, turtles, and pelagics. Best season April–November (calm seas). Base yourself at Bunaken Island itself or on Manado Tua/Siladen for shorter boat rides. Combine with Lembeh Strait (muck diving, macro photography) on the same trip.

The Derawan Islands (Kepulauan Derawan) in East Kalimantan are famous for stingless jellyfish lake on Kakaban, manta rays at Sangalaki, whale sharks at Talisayan, and green turtles nesting on Derawan. Access via Berau (BEJ) then a 2-hour speedboat. Remote, quiet, few international tourists. Best May–October.
